chapter_note: This chapter is predominantly cosmological teaching about why the Third Ambassador displayed his Image, how the rulers copied it to fashion Adam and Eve without the consent of Greatness, and how other composite life-forms arose without sexual intercourse. The only clear later layer is the disciples’ framed question (¶1) and a brief pedagogical closing (¶8). No NT citation formulas appear; the long “free woman” simile functions as an internal correspondential exposition rather than an institutional/pastoral application, though it may be a later rhetorical elaboration within the teaching tradition.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic/dialogue framing: disciples questioning the ‘glorious one’ with a report of intra-group opinion. Even though it rehearses cosmological facts, it is embedded as a framed dispute-question rather than impersonal exposition.

paragraphs.core_text: Regarding the Ambassador, the occasion when he came displaying his image, he [d]id not come so th[a]t he might reveal his image to the ru[l]ers in the universe. Rather, he came and displayed to the universe be[cause of h]is soul and his son, who is [ ... ] every [ ... ], that he might enable him to live [ ... ] and make for him a release; and to free (the soul) from every bond and all the fetters, in which it is entangled and bound.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue attribution/frame formula (“Then speaks the glorious one to his disciples:”) and manuscript page marker.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core cosmological mechanics (purpose of the Image-display as a salvific operation freeing the soul) embedded under a clear dialogue-attribution frame marker.

paragraphs.core_text: Still, you, look and see! The rulers and the authorities, in that they had no form in [ ... ] him, they lusted for his image. They reflected upon themselves, that [they] had no [one] like him in their creation. They sealed hi[s im]a[g]e in their heart, within their soul. Afterward[s, they] built it according to his likeness; they formed Adam and [Ev]e. They sealed the image of the exalted one in their [soul]. So, they [co]pied with an imitation; but they have not [copied i]n truth! Rather, just as [ ... ... ] it is made as these, for [i]t came [ ... ] but it is not l[ik]e him in truth. [Again, so too] is this figure of ma[nkind. They copi]ed it against the image of the exalted one [ ... ]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal cosmological causation (lust → sealing image → fashioning Adam/Eve) with ‘copy vs truth’ ontological distinction; no institutional pointing.

paragraphs.core_text: Similarly the [t]ree, for while it is like the [ ... it is] not [copi]ed in truth.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Brief correspondential analogy supporting the ‘likeness but not truth’ doctrine; stays generic and non-institutional.

paragraphs.core_text: This matt[er is comparable to] this: As a great, fre[e] woman [ ... ] within her [ ... ... ] rich in wealth [ ... ] po[ss]essions; she is also beautiful in her beauty, and is virtuous in her modesty. She walks in a free and reputable position. The fame of her beauty has spread in every c[i]ty. She sur[passes ... ] Behold h[er] chamber [ ... ] one who is mad, because [of] the nobles and the great ones. Al[so], they lust for her beautiful face. They did not [ ... ] her, because she is hidden in her palace [ ... ] within in a [ ... ] meet that woman [ ... ] his so[n]; or rather the head [ ... t]hat garment. This free woman shall [ ... ] leave the cha[mber] behind her and come to the street [ ... ] her head [ ... ] and she reveals her [face and her beauty ... ] because of her beloved broth[er]. This wom[an], on whom no man ever looked, nor did they ever see her fa[ce], as she neither desires nor rejoices [ ... ... ] leave her chamber behind her, and come in the midst of mankind [ ... ] and everyone view her. The hones[t] men and the nobles, even the servants too, and the [ ... ] look at her.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Extended simile/parable used to explain a cosmic act (voluntary display under constraint). Though it uses mundane imagery (woman, city, nobles), it functions as correspondential exposition rather than mapping to contemporary institutions.

paragraphs.core_text: In accord with this simile: Again, [this] too [is] how [ ... ] the Ambassador becomes [ ... ... ] as this free woman [ ... not] according to wantonness, in pride, nor [ ... she co]nsented to the outer world, she [ ... ... ], she revealed her face and her [beau]ty [ ... ] but only due to the constraint of grief [about] her [bel]ov[ed one].
paragraphs.temporal_note: Directly ties the parable back to the Ambassador’s cosmic action; explanatory, not exhortatory.

paragraphs.core_text: Now, this too is the way of the Third Ambassador, when he came and display[ed his] image with a show towards all the powers. [He did] not [co]me so that all the rulers and the author[it]ies would sculpt a form [after h]is likeness. R[ather], he came because of his son being crucified in the totality; [fo]r he would release him, free him, and rescue him from oppres-sion. Yet, when the rulers looked o[n] him, [th]ey lusted for his image. They fashioned after his [like]ness Adam and Eve, without the consent of the gre[at]ness.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core cosmological narrative: Third Ambassador’s Image-display as rescue operation; rulers’ lust produces Adam/Eve. ‘Crucified in the totality’ is the Manichaean cosmic Crucified One, not an NT citation.
Pedagogical wrap-up in second person (‘I have enlightened you… commit it to memory’) functioning as editorial/teacherly closure rather than cosmological mechanism.

paragraphs.core_text: [Understa]nd also this other (matter) that I will teach you. For, [a]s with Adam and Eve, whom the rulers fashioned and [se]aled after the image of the exalted one, so too this [i]s how a manifold divinity and many powers and angels [ ... received] the stamp of that image, which was displayed to them. For, in the majesty of the l[ig]ht and (the image's) love, they glowed with their desire and they were undone. Th[ey] were eager for their lust; like a m[an who looks] to the majesty of a lusted after face, and [ ... ] and he is eager for the [...] of the desire.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Systematic extension of the ‘Image-stamp’ mechanism to many cosmic beings; still internal to the cosmos. Contains simile language but not institutional application. Curly-brace artifact normalized to lacuna.

paragraphs.core_text: This is [als]o the case with those powers, when they looked on that majestic and beautiful [imag]e, they () [ ... ] a first image. They received the stamp of th[at image], which was displayed to them. They copied [ ... wh]ich th[ey co]pied out in a likeness, it being made [ ... ... ] the ones that they had put forth, which had received a [stamp of this im]age; but inward even to the rocks [ ... ... ] which occur from place to place. The [...] of that image, which was displayed in the universe [ ... ] they received a stamp, it being revealed there, and an impress.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal ‘stamping/copying’ cosmological process extended through grades of beings and even ‘rocks’; strongly expository. Curly-brace artifact normalized to lacuna.

paragraphs.core_text: Now, this new birth that they begot in a new [ ... ] in the world, is Adam and Eve. [There is not a] form in their world since the beginning like it; because that [im]age [occ]urs not in the worlds b[el]ow.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Cosmic ontological claim about the unprecedented form and its origin in the displayed Image; ‘new birth’ is descriptive, not institutional/pastoral.

paragraphs.core_text: Not all the figures that have been fashioned were fashioned by birth from displayed intercourse. Rather, there are other figures fashioned [ ... ]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Programmatic cosmological thesis introducing non-sexual generation of forms; impersonal and classificatory.

paragraphs.core_text: One of them is the sea [gi]ant, the 'sweeping' from the sphere, which the [Father] of Life discharged into the sea. Its own fire and thought fashioned it [in] a figure.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Cosmic exemplar with named being (Father of Life) and internal faculties (‘fire and thought’) as formative forces—substrate-style mechanism.

paragraphs.core_text: The second figure is the one [that] fell to the earth. It made the sea its womb. Its own l[us]t became its sculptor. It alone fashioned it to a nature, which is the root of death. Yet, when it came up from the sea, it [ ... ] that it might destroy the works [ ... ] of Life. They immediately sent against it the Adamant of Light, the great 'instruction of vigour'. He humbled it in the districts of the north. He has trampled underfoot and set h[im]self upon it, until the end of the world.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Fully cosmological combat-mechanics and personified agents (Adamant of Light) with geographic cosmic locale (‘districts of the north’); no contemporary referents.

paragraphs.core_text: [The] third figure is the nature that fell on wh[at] is dr[y. It] fashioned the tree and set itself there. [ ... the] new figure that was fashioned [ ... d]isplays.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Third cosmological exemplar (vegetation/tree) framed as another non-sexual ‘fashioning’; remains within cosmic process language.

paragraphs.core_text: So, in accord with the essence they [ ... the Dark]ness; but yet th[ey] did not come with the King of Dark[ness to the wo]rld. Rather, their fashioning [came] about [ ... ] they are composite and have been displayed in the world.
paragraphs.temporal_note: General doctrinal conclusion: composite forms not simply imported by the King of Darkness but arising in-world; impersonal, ontological register. Capitalized Darkness as a cosmic principle/agent.
